chunks: "Hysteresis means a circuit has two different switching thresholds depending on which way the input is moving.
On the way up, the output flips at an upper threshold V T plus ; on the way down it flips at a lower threshold V T- . The gap between them is the hysteresis.
You get it with positive feedback. In a comparator, you feed a fraction of the output back to the non-inverting input through a resistor divider.
When the output is high it pushes the reference up a bit; when it's low it pulls it down.
So once the output has switched, the input has to move back past the opposite threshold, not just the same one, to switch it back.
Why use it: if the input is slow or noisy, with a single threshold the output would toggle every time noise carried it across.
With hysteresis wider than the noise, the output switches once.
That's what Schmitt-trigger inputs do on microcontroller pins, button debouncing, slow sensor inputs, and I²C inputs.
The cost is some delay and a dead band, and if the noise is bigger than the window, it still chatters."
